---
title: "Release chain"
description: "From a dev → main pull request to a drafted GitHub release, automatically."
---

A release needs two caller files. Together they turn a pull request from
`dev` into `main` into a merged PR and a drafted release — the only manual
step is opening the PR.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  pr(["PR: dev → main"]) --> check["R CMD check"]
  check -- "success" --> merge["Merge PR"]
  check -- "failure" --> issue["Issue for the PR author"]
  merge --> trigger["Trigger release"]
  trigger -. "repository_dispatch:<br/>release-publish" .-> publish["Publish release<br/>(second caller)"]
```

## 1. Release trigger

Runs on the pull request into `main`. It checks the package, merges the PR
if the check passes (or opens an issue if it fails), and then starts the
release.

{{< example release-trigger.yml >}}

The `if: github.head_ref == 'dev'` guard skips everything for PRs from other
branches; [Require head branch](require-head-branch.qmd) additionally blocks
them from being merged.

## 2. Publish release

Listens for the `release-publish` event and runs
[semantic-release](package-release.qmd) on `main`.

{{< example release-publish.yml >}}

## Why two files?

semantic-release refuses to release from a run triggered by a pull
request, and the first file has to be one — the checks and the merge belong
to the PR. So after merging, it sends a `repository_dispatch` event, which
starts the second file as a **new, independent run** on the merged `main`.

This works with the default `GITHUB_TOKEN`: events it creates normally don't
start new workflow runs, but `repository_dispatch` is an explicit exception.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Trying it out without releasing
Set `dry-run: true` in the publish caller. The whole chain runs — including
the merge — but the release step only reports the next version and the
release notes in its log. Remove the line before your first real release.
:::
